title: Back again
goal: Greet someone you have not seen for a long time, and talk precisely about time: how long ago, since when, for how long, and what has only just happened. Indonesian does all of it without a single tense.
bekal: say how long something has lasted with *selama* and *sudah … (lamanya)*
say since when with *sejak*, and what has only just happened with *baru saja*
place events either side of today: *tiga bulan yang lalu*, *seminggu lagi*, *lusa*, *semalam*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ketemu lagi di bandara
dialogs.intro: Yogyakarta International Airport, a Saturday afternoon at the start of January 2027, fourteen months after Sarah flew home. Rina has come from Jakarta for the weekend to welcome her back; Sarah's connecting flight from Bali is late.

lines.text: Rina! Sudah lama tidak ketemu!
lines.id: Rina! Long time no see!
lines.literal: Rina! already long not meet!

lines.text: Lama banget! Aku nunggu di sini sejak jam dua, lho.

lines.text: Maaf, Rin. Pesawatnya terlambat hampir satu jam.

lines.text: Pantesan makin lancar! Kantor Yogya kan baru buka tiga bulan yang lalu.

lines.text: Iya. Sejak Pak Hendra menelepon saya, saya hampir tidak bisa tidur.

lines.text: Senang banget, ya? Terus, kamu tinggal di mana?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Di Prawirotaman. Saya mengontrak rumah kecil di sana selama setahun.
lines.id: In Prawirotaman. I'm renting a little house there for a year.

lines.text: Asyik! Aku di sini sampai lusa. Nanti malam kita makan gudeg, ya!
lines.id: Brilliant! I'm here till the day after tomorrow. Tonight we're having gudeg!

notes: **Sudah lama tidak ketemu!** is the standard "long time no see". In speech it shrinks to *Lama nggak ketemu!* or just *Lama banget!* *Ketemu* is the everyday word for *bertemu* (to meet): you will hear it far more often, but in writing use *bertemu*.

**Ya ampun** is surprise, delight or dismay: "oh my goodness". It comes from a plea for God's forgiveness (*ampun* = mercy), but nobody hears religion in it any more, just as nobody hears it in English "goodness me".

**Aku nunggu** — Rina talks like the Jakartan she is: *aku* for "I", *nggak* for *tidak*, and *nunggu* for *menunggu* (to wait). Squashing the *me-* prefix like this is how people actually speak. Units 2 and 3 show you exactly how the prefix works, spoken and written.

**Ngapain aja?** is "what have you been up to?" *Ngapain* is spoken Indonesian for "doing what" (standard *melakukan apa*), and *aja* (*saja*) here means "all the various things", not "only". ⚠️ The same word can also mean "why on earth": *Ngapain ke sana?* — why would you go there?

**Pantesan** means "no wonder", from standard *pantas*. You say it when one fact suddenly explains another: *Pantesan macet, ada banjir* — no wonder the traffic's bad, there's a flood. Bu Endang will use the short form, *pantes*.

**Mengontrak rumah** is renting a whole house on a yearly contract, usually paid for the entire year up front. A *rumah kontrakan* (or just *kontrakan*) is the step up from the *kos* Sarah had in Jakarta: your own house, your own gate, and your own leaking roof.

grammars.title: Since, for, and how long
body: English needs "for", "since" and the present perfect ("I have been waiting"). Indonesian does the same job with a handful of little words and leaves the verb alone.
after: *Lamanya* ("its length") is optional and slightly bookish; *Sudah empat belas bulan* says the same. Putting the period first adds weight: *Sudah dua tahun saya tinggal di sini* — I've lived here for two years now.

⚠️ Don't translate a "for" of time that has passed as *untuk*. *Saya tinggal di Jakarta untuk setahun* is English in disguise; say *selama setahun*. *Untuk* works only for a period you are planning: *kontrak untuk dua tahun*.

*Sejak* and *selama* can also introduce a whole clause, not just a time: *sejak Pak Hendra menelepon saya* (ever since Pak Hendra rang me), *selama saya di Melbourne* (the whole time I was in Melbourne). No extra word is needed.

grammars.title: Ago and in: yang lalu and lagi
body: Almost every time word has a partner on the other side of today. Learn them in pairs and you have doubled your vocabulary for free.
after: *Lagi* after a period of time means "from now": *seminggu lagi* is "in a week's time". It can also mean "another": *minta seminggu lagi* is to ask for one more week. The situation always decides.
💬 In speech *yang lalu* is often cut to *lalu*: *tiga bulan lalu*. Both are correct; the longer form is what you write.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Di depan pagar
dialogs.intro: Sunday morning. Rina has gone to find breakfast, and Sarah is opening the gate of her new house when her landlady, who lives next door, comes out with a broom.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Pagi! Ini Mbak Sarah, to?

lines.literal: morning! this Miss Sarah, [to]?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Betul, Bu. Ibu pasti Bu Endang.
lines.id: That's right. You must be Bu Endang.

lines.text: Nggih, saya Endang. Kapan sampai, Mbak?
lines.id: Yes, I'm Endang. When did you arrive?

lines.text: Wah, capek, to. Bahasa Indonesianya kok lancar, Mbak? Sudah berapa lama belajar?
lines.id: Of course, you must have been tired. How come your Indonesian's so fluent? How long have you been learning?
lines.literal: wah, tired, [to]. language Indonesia-the [kok] fluent, miss? already how-much long learn?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Sudah dua tahun lebih, Bu. Dulu saya kerja setahun di Jakarta.
lines.id: Just over two years. I used to work in Jakarta, for a year.
lines.literal: already two year more, ma'am. formerly I work one-year at Jakarta.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Oh, pantes. Saya di kampung ini sejak menikah, tahun delapan puluh tujuh.
lines.id: Ah, that explains it. I've been in this kampung since I got married, in eighty-seven.
lines.literal: oh, no-wonder. I at kampung this since marry, year eight ten seven.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Wah, berarti sudah empat puluh tahun, ya, Bu.
lines.id: Goodness, so that's forty years.
lines.literal: wow, means already four ten year, yes, ma'am.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Nggih. Kalau butuh apa-apa, bilang saja. Rumah saya persis di sebelah.
lines.id: Yes. If you need anything, just say. My house is right next door.
lines.literal: yes. if need what-what, say just. house my exactly at beside.

lines.text: Terima kasih banyak, Bu. Mari, Bu, saya ke warung dulu.
lines.id: Thank you so much. Excuse me, I'm just popping to the shop.

lines.text: Monggo, monggo. Hati-hati, Mbak.
lines.id: Go ahead, go ahead. Take care.

notes: **To** at the end of a sentence is Javanese, and in Yogyakarta it is everywhere. It works like the English tag "…, aren't you?" or the Indonesian *kan*: *Ini Mbak Sarah, to?* expects a yes. You don't need to use it, but you must recognise it.

**Nggih** is the polite Javanese *ya*. Older people in Yogya drop it into Indonesian sentences as a mark of courtesy. Answering an elder with *nggih* is charming from a foreigner; answering with *iya* is perfectly correct.
**Semalam** has two meanings: "last night" (as here) and "one night" (*menginap semalam*, to stay one night). *Tadi malam* means only "last night", and it is what you will hear more often in Jakarta.

**Bahasa Indonesianya kok lancar?** Indonesians compliment your language constantly, sometimes after two words. *Kok* marks surprise ("how come…?"). The gracious reply is modest: *Ah, masih belajar, Bu* — oh, I'm still learning.

**Tahun delapan puluh tujuh** — in formal speech a year is read as a whole number (*seribu sembilan ratus delapan puluh tujuh*), but people shorten it just as English does. *Tahun delapan puluhan* is "the eighties".

**Mari, Bu … Monggo.** When you leave someone or walk past them, *Mari* (roughly "let me be on my way") is the polite way to excuse yourself. The reply is *Mari* again or, in Java, *Monggo* ("please, go ahead"). In a kampung you will say *mari* ten times a day.

grammars.title: Asking how long, answering with baru or sudah
body: The question words from Dialogue 1, now as a conversation kit. Watch the first word of each answer: it tells you how the speaker feels about the number.

head: Question
Answer
English
rows: When did you arrive? Yesterday afternoon.
How long have you been in Yogya? Only two days.
How long have you been learning? Over two years.
Since when have you lived here? Since 1987.
How long were you in Jakarta? A year.
How long are you here for? Till the day after tomorrow.

after: *Baru dua hari* means "only two days so far"; *sudah dua hari* means "two days already". Same number, opposite feeling. *Baru saja* goes one step further: it happened moments ago, as in *Rina baru saja pergi* — Rina has just left.
*Lebih* after a number means "and a bit": *dua tahun lebih*, *jam tiga lebih* (just after three). Put it before the number and it means "more than": *lebih dari dua tahun*.

blocks.text: Indonesian slices the day by the light and the heat, not by the clock, and the slices don't match English "morning" and "afternoon". *Siang* is the hot middle of the day; *sore* begins when the heat starts to ease.

blocks.title: Late, on time, and rubber time
items: *terlambat* is the standard word for late; *telat* is what people say. Flights are *delay* (said *DI-lé*), borrowed straight from airport English.
*tepat waktu* is on time; *molor* is when an event stretches and starts late; *ngaret* (from *karet*, rubber) is being habitually late.
*jam karet* — rubber time — is the national joke about punctuality. Offices, flights and official ceremonies increasingly run on time, so don't rely on it.

blocks.text: *Pagi ini* and *tadi pagi* both translate as "this morning", but *pagi ini* can be said while it is still morning, and *tadi pagi* only once it is over. The same logic separates *malam ini* (tonight, from now on) and *nanti malam* (tonight, later on).

sections.title: Coming back: what people will say to you

blocks.text: Come back anywhere in Indonesia after a long absence and you will hear the same handful of lines. They are friendly rituals, not questions that need long answers.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Remarks about your body
items: *Gemukan, ya?* (put on weight, haven't you?) and *Kok hitam sekarang?* (you've gone so brown!) are small talk, not insults. Weight and skin are ordinary topics.
Laugh, say *Ah, masa?* (really?) or *Iya, nih, kebanyakan makan* (yes, eating too much), and move on.
Don't return the remark. It is the foreigner who comments back who ends up sounding rude.
